title: Optimal Hyperparameters for Differentially Private Transfer Learning
one_liner: When training a model on private data, the clipping bound and batch size must be chosen differently than textbook theory suggests—cumulative noise and gradient distributions, not fixed heuristics, reveal which numbers actually work.
lead: When you train a model on sensitive data (medical records, financial data, personal images), you add noise to protect individual privacy. But this noise creates a puzzle: the math says one thing about how to choose the noise amount, yet in practice you get better results doing the opposite. This paper figures out why—by treating clipping (the noise-adding step) as a re-weighting of gradients (the direction nudges) and tracking cumulative noise (total noise over all training steps), not just single-step noise.

paras: Start with a pretrained model (e.g., a vision model trained on millions of public images). You want to adapt it to a specific task using private data—say, classifying rare plant diseases from a farmer's own photos. The issue: you must add noise during training to protect each photo's privacy, but noise harms learning.

Textbook theory says: stronger privacy (which means more noise) requires clipping gradients more aggressively—cutting off the largest direction nudges. But in real experiments (measured from actual training runs), this is backward. More aggressive clipping makes the model worse, because it removes the very gradient nudges that convey the most learning signal about which way the model should move.

Existing recipes for choosing batch size (how many examples per update step) also fail. They ignore a hard fact: in practice, you have a fixed compute budget—say, run training for exactly 10 epochs, no more. Under that constraint, the standard heuristics pick batch sizes that either waste compute or introduce too much variance.

callout.html: Stronger privacy needs smaller clipping (theory says protect more, cut more), yet in real experiments (measured from actual training runs) larger clipping works better because the gradient distribution shifts under noise—and standard batch-size recipes fail under fixed compute because they count per-step noise instead of total noise across all steps.

panels.caption: Gradient norms spread across a wide range—some nudges are large, some tiny.

panels.title: 2. Theory says: clip tight

panels.caption: But under privacy noise, gradient distribution shifts—nudges cluster differently.

panels.title: 4. Clipping re-weights them
panels.viz_args: big nudges cut | small nudges pass → effectively down-weight big movers
panels.caption: Clipping does not just limit size—it re-weights which gradients matter.

panels.title: 5. Cumulative noise decides
panels.caption: Larger batches add fewer noisy updates but noisier each; total noise over training decides best batch size.

steps.text: Measure how the typical size of gradient nudges changes when privacy noise is added, across different clipping choices.
View clipping not as truncation but as assigning different importance to different gradients—large nudges penalized, small nudges unchanged.

Show mathematically that clipping to minimize MSE (squared difference between clipped and original nudge) directly improves training progress per step, because smaller mismatch means the actual direction nudges steer the model more faithfully toward the loss minimum.

steps.b: Step 4: Count cumulative noise over epochs
steps.text: Instead of fixing the number of steps, fix the number of training epochs—then track total noise accumulated across all steps.

steps.b: Step 5: Choose batch size by noise budget
steps.text: Pick the batch size that achieves minimum cumulative noise without dropping below a minimum number of steps required for convergence.

paras: The paper changes how you choose two numbers: the clipping bound (how far to cut each gradient nudge) and the batch size (how many examples per update). Instead of applying one fixed recipe across all tasks, it derives rules that adapt to privacy budget, model capability, and compute constraints.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: cumulative DP noise
hidden.name: Cumulative DP noise
paras: Cumulative DP noise is the total amount of randomness added to gradient nudges, summed across every training step. When you set batch size high, each step is noisier (noise spread across fewer examples), but you take fewer steps. When batch size is small, each step is less noisy, but you take more steps. The total noise across all steps—the sum, not the average—is what actually matters for privacy-utility tradeoff.

The paper estimates cumulative noise by computing how much variance (squared randomness) accumulates as training proceeds, then choosing the batch size that minimizes this sum without forcing convergence to fail. It differs from prior work, which only looked at noise per step—missing that many small-noise steps (high total noise from many steps) versus few large-noise steps (high per-step noise but few of them) have different cumulative totals, and the option with lower cumulative total wins because noise compounds over steps.

heat.caption: Darker means more cumulative noise. Small batches accumulate noise fast (many noisy steps); large batches accumulate noise slower but noisier per step.

reads.html: Cumulative noise is the total randomness injected across all your training steps. If you take 100 noisy steps, each adding 10 units of noise, that is 1000 units total—and is worse than 10 steps with noise spread so each step is noisier but fewer of them, because the total randomness across all steps is what determines privacy loss and learning degradation.

The cumulative DP noise is formalized as the sum of mean-squared errors (MSE) of clipped-versus-unclipped gradients, weighted by the privacy-amplification factor, across all optimization steps. Minimizing this under a constraint on minimum steps for convergence predicts batch-size performance better than prior per-step heuristics, because the total compounding of noise matters more for learning than the noise in any single step.

mechanism.h2: Why the standard approach fails and the paper fixes it
paras: Standard theory assumes you can pick a clipping bound by analyzing a single step in isolation—choosing the number that minimizes noise per step. But this misses something important: when privacy noise is added, the distribution of gradient nudges shifts. The nudges that were previously large might become medium, and the tiny ones stay tiny. Clipping now acts as a re-weighting: cutting the large nudges penalizes the parts of the model that move most strongly, while leaving weak nudges unchanged.

The paper shows mathematically that clipping to minimize mean-squared error (the squared difference between the clipped and the original nudge) directly improves the upper bound on how much the loss shrinks per training step, because smaller mismatch means the clipped nudges steer more faithfully toward the loss minimum. This is why empirically larger clipping often works: it re-weights the gradients in a way that matches the actual distribution under noise, avoiding the overcutting that theory (which ignores distribution shifts) predicts.

For batch size, standard heuristics fix the number of training steps and ask: which batch size gives the best noise-to-signal ratio per step? But when compute is truly bounded (fixed epochs, not fixed steps), that rule breaks. A larger batch means fewer steps—you take fewer noisy nudges, but each is noisier. A tiny batch means many steps—each is less noisy, but the total noise from all those steps compounds. The paper counts cumulative noise: across all steps you will take, how much total randomness do you add? The best batch size is the one that minimizes cumulative noise while still taking enough steps for the model to learn.

stages.s: Private data + pretrained model + privacy budget + compute limit
Measure gradient norms at different clipping levels
Reframe clipping as re-weighting (minimize MSE per step)
Compute cumulative noise across all possible batch sizes
Choose batch size minimizing cumulative noise with enough steps
Optimal clipping bound and batch size for your task

math.h2: The core equation: loss improvement bounds
math.words: Expected loss improvement = loss gradient magnitude squared minus mean-squared error of clipping (scaled by step size)
symbols: the model weights at step t
step size (how far to nudge the weights)
gradient (direction to nudge to reduce loss)
mean-squared error: squared difference between clipped gradient and true gradient, when clipping bound is C
clipping bound (how far to cut each gradient)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose at step t the true gradient is 50 (a nudge direction). With clipping bound C=10, the clipped gradient is 10.
If you increase C to 30: clipped gradient is 30, MSE = (50-30)^2 = 400. Loss improvement = 1.25 - 0.2 = 1.05 (better).
The better clipping (larger C matching the actual gradient distribution) makes larger per-step progress—explaining why empirically larger C often wins under privacy.

math.note: The equation says: loss shrinks by the gradient's strength, minus a penalty for how badly clipping mismatch the true direction. Clipping to minimize this mismatch—often larger clipping than theory predicts—makes training progress per step larger.

charts.title: Standard heuristic (fixed-steps)
charts.note: Standard batch-size rules work under loose privacy but collapse under tight privacy because they assume fixed steps.

charts.title: This paper (cumulative noise, fixed epochs)
charts.note: By tracking cumulative noise and adapting batch size to the compute budget, performance stays good across privacy levels.

items.html: If you use textbook clipping advice without measuring how gradient norms actually change under privacy in your specific task, you will clip too aggressively or too loosely. The optimal clipping depends on your pretrained model, data, and privacy budget.

Using the same clipping bound and batch size for multiple tasks (e.g., all vision fine-tuning jobs) leads to suboptimal performance on some tasks, because different tasks have different gradient distributions—a model that struggles to learn on sparse data needs different clipping than one fine-tuning on abundant data, and stronger privacy budgets shift the optimal trade-offs.
Optimizing only for per-step noise-to-signal ratio ignores that a tiny batch means many steps and their noise compounds. A larger batch with higher per-step noise can have lower cumulative noise.
Measure gradient norms and cumulative noise for your task, adapt clipping and batch size to your privacy budget and compute limit, and test across privacy settings to verify performance stays good.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a private fine-tuning experiment: take a pretrained vision model (e.g., ViT-Base pretrained on ImageNet), add noise to gradients, and fine-tune on a small private dataset (e.g., 10 percent of CIFAR-100). Sweep over clipping bounds (try 1, 2, 5, 10, 20) and batch sizes (try 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) while keeping epochs fixed. For each pair, compute: (1) final accuracy on the private task, (2) mean-squared error of the clipping, and (3) cumulative DP noise over training. Plot accuracy versus cumulative noise for each batch size. The demo proves the paper by showing that the batch size minimizing cumulative noise matches the one with highest accuracy, contradicting standard heuristics.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = correct predictions on private test set / total test examples
demo.closing: The core result: the batch size that minimizes cumulative noise over all training steps, not per-step noise, predicts which batch size actually works best for learning on private data.
